sources.news_title: Tropical Depression Nine Formed in Gulf of Mexico
sources.text:
El Centro Nacional de Huracanes (CNH) de Estados Unidos reportó la formación de la Depresión Tropical Nueve frente a las costas de Veracruz y Tamaulipas, con vientos máximos sostenidos de 55 kilómetros por hora.
En un aviso, el organismo informó que el sistema se desplaza hacia el este, aunque se espera que durante los próximos dos días cambie su trayectoria hacia el noreste y posteriormente gire en esa dirección el viernes.
"En la trayectoria del pronóstico, se espera que la depresión pase al norte de la Península de Yucatán el jueves y se acerque a la costa norte del Golfo (de México), en Estados Unidos, el viernes", apuntó el CNH. El organismo pronosticó un fortalecimiento constante del sistema, por lo que se espera que se convierta en tormenta tropical durante las primeras horas del miércoles y alcance la categoría de huracán el jueves.
Ante este escenario, el Servicio Meteorológico Nacional (SMN) previó para esta tarde y noche lluvias puntuales intensas, de 75 a 150 milímetros, acompañadas de descargas eléctricas y rachas de viento en Tamaulipas, Veracruz y Puebla.
Además de este sistema, el CNH mantiene bajo vigilancia una zona de baja presión frente a las costas de Oaxaca, cuya probabilidad de desarrollo ciclónico aumentó a 90 por ciento para las próximas 48 horas. De acuerdo con el organismo estadounidense, las condiciones ambientales son favorables para un desarrollo gradual y es probable que el sistema se convierta en depresión tropical durante el próximo día, mientras se desplaza lentamente hacia el oeste-noroeste. "Independientemente del desarrollo, se esperan fuertes lluvias en porciones del sur y suroeste de México durante los próximos días", advirtió el CNH.

sources.news_title: First Atlantic Hurricane of 2026 Seen Threatening US Gulf Coast
sources.text:
The US Gulf Coast will likely be hit by the first Atlantic hurricane of the year in coming days by a storm now gathering strength off the Mexican coast.
A tropical depression, the first step in a storm’s evolution to hurricane status, formed about 630 miles south of the Mississippi River’s mouth with winds of 35 miles per hour, the US National Hurricane Center said in a 5 p.m. New York time advisory. 
The system is expected to become Tropical Storm Isaias by Wednesday and progress to hurricane strength by Thursday.
“Residents from Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle should closely monitor the latest forecast updates and ensure they have their hurricane plan in place,” John Cangialosi, a senior hurricane specialist at the center, wrote in his outlook. “The system will bring areas of heavy rainfall to the central US Gulf coast Friday into the weekend.”
Current track forecasts take the storm to the east of the major offshore oil and natural gas production south of Louisiana and Texas, although there could be some disruptions depending its path and size. If the forecast holds, winds will peak at 100 mph, making it a Category 2 hurricane on the five-step, Saffir-Simpson scale. It would be the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, a milestone normally reached in the second week of August. 
This Atlantic season has lagged well behind the usual pace, with eight named storms, none of which became hurricanes. By early October, an average season typically has produced about 11 named storms, including five hurricanes and two major hurricanes.
Strengthening El Niño conditions have increased wind shear that helped suppress activity across the basin. Shear occurs when winds change speed or direction at different altitudes, disrupting a storm’s structure. 
The warm waters of the Gulf will fuel the storm, Cangialosi said. 
“Based on the environmental conditions and the model guidance, the cyclone will likely peak in strength before reaching the coast,” he said. 
In addition to high winds, the storm is expected to drop as much as 6 inches of rain across the Gulf states, with some isolated areas getting up to 10 inches, the hurricane center said.

Tropical Depression Nine to strengthen into Category Two Hurricane in Gulf
With end of hurricane season weeks away, tropical threat brewing in Gulf could impact U.S. this weekend
sources.text:
Tropical threat brewing in Gulf could impact U.S. as a hurricane this weekend. See maps, possible path.
With less than two months remaining in the 2026 hurricane season, the potential for a ninth named tropical storm in the Atlantic basin is brewing in the southern Gulf.
Since the Atlantic's season began on June 1, it has only seen eight named storms this year, while El Niño continues to bring a more active season in the Pacific. The season ends Nov. 30.
What we know about the possible path
Tropical Depression Nine formed in the Gulf on Tuesday. As the storm brews over the warmer waters off Mexico, it's expected to become a tropical storm by early Wednesday and a hurricane on Thursday, according to the National Hurricane Center.
If it does become a tropical storm, it would receive the name Isaias, pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs."
Forecast models are beginning to come to agreement that the northward motion of this tropical system brings it to the Gulf Coast this weekend.
Regardless of its name or if it develops into a tropical storm, we do know that it will bring moderate to heavy rainfall to the Gulf Coast and into the rest of the Southeast this weekend into early next week.
Some longer-range forecast models also see this moisture eventually reaching the Ohio Valley and Northeast by midweek next week.
What we do not know
Timing, storm intensity and severity of impacts to land with this tropical system are what remain unknown.
While some models have impacts starting Friday evening, others show it beginning later in the weekend.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis on Tuesday signed an executive order declaring a state of emergency for 25 Florida counties ahead of the storm's arrival. DeSantis said in a statement that the order "ensures communities have the time and resources necessary to prepare for potential severe weather impacts to the Panhandle and Big Bend region of Florida."
Beware the "I"-named storm
While tropical storm and hurricane formation and frequency vary throughout the season, the "I"-named systems tend to be the most retired names within the Atlantic basin.
The most commonly known retired "I"-named storms are Ian (2022), Ida (2021), Irma (2017), and Irene (2011).
When Ike was retired in 2008, Isaias replaced the "I" name on the Atlantic tropical cyclones list, which rotates every six years.

sources.news_title: National Hurricane Center Tracking Gulf Disturbance That Could Approach Florida Panhandle
sources.text:
The National Hurricane Center (NHC) is tracking a disturbance in the southwestern Gulf of Mexico that could move toward the Florida Panhandle and other parts of the northern Gulf Coast later this week.
The system, designated AL92, had a 90% chance of developing into a tropical cyclone within 48 hours and over the next seven days, according to the NHC’s Oct. 6 outlook.
Forecasters said showers and thunderstorms associated with a broad area of low pressure were becoming better organized, and a tropical depression could form within about a day as the system moves generally eastward.
The NHC expects the disturbance to eventually turn north or northeast toward the northern Gulf Coast. The agency specifically advised interests from the Florida Panhandle westward to Louisiana to monitor the system.
It remained too early Tuesday to determine whether the disturbance would make landfall in Florida or what specific impacts the state could experience. The NHC had not issued a Florida landfall forecast, and the system had not yet strengthened into a tropical depression or named storm.

sources.news_title: Tropical Depression Nine forms in the Gulf, expected to strengthen quickly - WXXV News 25
sources.text:
Tropical Depression Nine forms in the Gulf, expected to strengthen quickly
Meteorologist Sam Lucey has a look at the forecast for south Mississippi
Tropical Depression Nine has formed over the Gulf of America and is expected to strengthen quickly as it moves east, then turns northeast toward the northern Gulf Coast.
As of 4 p.m. Tuesday, the system was about 630 miles southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi River, with maximum sustained winds of 35 mph. It was moving east at about 5 mph.
The depression is expected to become a tropical storm by early Wednesday and a hurricane by Thursday. The forecast track takes the system north of the Yucatan Peninsula Thursday before it turns northeast and approaches the U.S. northern Gulf Coast Friday.
There are currently no coastal watches or warnings in effect, but interests along the northern Gulf Coast should closely monitor the system.
Rain could become the biggest concern
Rainfall will increase across the Gulf Coast as the system approaches. From Friday through the weekend, 3 to 6 inches of rain is forecast across portions of the central Gulf Coast, from southeastern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle, with localized totals up to 10 inches possible.
That could lead to flash flooding, urban flooding and some river flooding, especially where heavier rain bands persist.
For the Mississippi and Alabama Gulf Coasts, the exact track and strength will determine where the heaviest rain and strongest winds set up. Conditions are expected to become increasingly unsettled late this week, with the greatest impacts possible Friday into the weekend.
We will continue to track the system closely as it strengthens and moves toward the northern Gulf Coast.

sources.news_title: Tropical depression in Gulf forecast to become hurricane
sources.text:
US News
Tropical depression in Gulf forecast to become hurricane
Tropical Depression Nine is forecast to become the Atlantic season’s first hurricane and reach the U.S. Gulf Coast as a dangerous storm, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC). The system would be named Isaias when it strengthens into a tropical storm.
The depression had maximum sustained winds of 35 mph at 4 p.m. CT Tuesday and was about 630 miles southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi River, according to the NHC. It was moving east at 5 mph, according to the hurricane center’s first advisory.
Forecasters expect it to become a tropical storm by early Wednesday and a hurricane Thursday. The system is expected to pass north of Mexico’s Yucatan Peninsula on Thursday before turning northeast and approaching the northern Gulf Coast on Friday.
Conditions appear generally favorable for strengthening over the next few days. The hurricane center said the cyclone’s compact size could help it strengthen steadily, and some reliable forecast models show a stronger storm than the official forecast.
The system will likely reach its peak strength before arriving at the coast. Increasing vertical wind shear could cause some weakening as it approaches land.
“But it is still expected to be a dangerous hurricane when it makes landfall,” the hurricane center said.
The storm is also expected to grow significantly in size as it reaches the northern Gulf Coast, particularly on its eastern side. Forecasters cautioned people against focusing on individual points along the forecast track because of uncertainty and the storm’s expected growth.
National Weather Service (NWS) meteorologist Donald Jones in Lake Charles, Louisiana, said preliminary estimates pointed to a possible landfall along coastal southeastern Louisiana, Mississippi or Alabama. An official hurricane center forecast track was not yet available when he spoke.
The forecast follows a record delay in the Atlantic’s first hurricane of the season in the satellite era. Eight named tropical storms have formed this year, but none has reached the 74 mph sustained-wind threshold required to become a hurricane.

ORLANDO, Fla. – Tropical Depression Nine has formed in the Southern Gulf in the Bay of Campeche. It is expected to drift eastward before being pulled north by a trough of low pressure over Texas. This will steer it to a likely landfall near the Louisiana coastline.
Environmental conditions do look conducive for further strengthening in the short term. Tropical Storm Isaias is likely to form in the Central Gulf Tuesday evening. This will become the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic Hurricane Season. As this system nears the northern Gulf Coast, it will interact with more upper level shear from the trough of low pressure. This will weaken it slightly before landfall.
While this will not make a direct impact for Central Florida, we will feel indirect effects from this system. As TD9/Isaias nears landfall, it will begin to drag deep tropical moisture from the Caribbean and funnel it into Central Florida. This will keep our rain chances high through the weekend. It will not be until early next week that drier air begins to make a comeback in the area.

sources.news_title: Invest 92L may be setting its sights on Florida Panhandle
Tropical Depression 9 could become season’s first hurricane, threatening Gulf Coast
sources.text:
The National Hurricane Center has officially labeled Invest 92L as Tropical Depression Nine, and it is likely to become our first hurricane of the season before making landfall, probably along the central Gulf Coast, sometime between Friday night and Saturday morning.
We have been monitoring this area for days, and over the last 24 to 36 hours, we have noticed that the low-pressure area that developed on Monday has become better organized. Hurricane hunters, specifically the NOAA Gulfstream jet, have been flying around the system and will continue to investigate it throughout the evening. Hurricane hunters from the Air Force Reserve's 53rd Weather Reconnaissance Squadron are expected to investigate the system on Wednesday morning.
Tue Oct 6: Here is the latest update on newly formed Tropical Depression #Nine from the National Hurricane Center:
TD #Nine in the western Gulf is forecast to strengthen. There is an increasing risk of dangerous wind & storm surge impacts along portions of the northern Gulf… pic.twitter.com/OT6Gd4Nc21
— National Hurricane Center (@NHC_Atlantic) October 6, 2026
The first advisory issued by the National Hurricane Center at 5 p.m. on Tuesday indicates that the system has maximum sustained winds of 35 mph and is moving east at around 5 mph. No coastal watches or warnings are currently in effect, but this will likely change as early as Wednesday evening across parts of the Gulf Coast.
First, some areas can expect tropical storm watches, which could be upgraded to warnings on Thursday or Friday. The tropical depression is expected to continue moving east-northeast during the next couple of days. By Friday, the system should start turning northeast as it approaches the northern Gulf Coast of the United States.
In the short term, between Tuesday evening and Thursday morning, the system is expected to move at less than 10 mph. Once the system makes that northward turn, it should start picking up speed as steering winds influence it.
A little concerning that the GFS trended much stronger/faster with #TD9 after getting some G-IV data assimilated. The shear near the Gulf coast isn't going away, but the stronger this gets earlier, the more it might be able to resist some of that. https://t.co/HrXdo05NYj pic.twitter.com/mKMoIHyKBS
— Andy Hazelton (@AndyHazelton) October 6, 2026
Sea surface temperatures are running around 1.8°F above average for this time of year across the Gulf. There is not only plenty of warm water, but it also extends very deep. Therefore, there is plenty of fuel available for the system to intensify. The main factor working against this system is strong wind shear dropping from the continental United States toward the Southeast. So, even though the system has plenty of time and warm water to intensify, wind shear could definitely limit its development.
What are the possible impacts to Florida?
Florida will continue to receive heavy rain through much of this week. Remember, the rain we have been receiving this week has mainly been due to local effects across the southern half of Florida, as well as a stationary frontal boundary across Central Florida, North Florida, and the Panhandle. This frontal boundary will continue to meander around the region at least through Thursday, so expect periods of heavy rain that could lead to flash flooding in some areas.
The Weather Prediction Center continues to place portions of Florida, especially areas from Central Florida through the Lake Okeechobee region, under a marginal risk for flash flooding. By Friday into Saturday, the Weather Prediction Center highlights the western portion of the Panhandle, from areas just west and south of Tallahassee through Pensacola, under a slight risk for flash flooding due to the approaching tropical system.
Florida needs to closely monitor any shift in the track toward the east, as a closer path could potentially bring rounds of heavy rain across the Peninsula. As of Tuesday, the forecast track is far enough west for much of Florida to receive only sporadic rain bands associated with the system. If the system's path shifts farther east, however, we could see more persistent rainfall and a higher threat of tornadoes.
The National Hurricane Center reports rainfall totals of around 4 to 6 inches from Tropical Depression Nine across the western Panhandle. Parts of the Tampa Bay area could also receive around 4 inches of rain.
We will continue to monitor any changes closely and bring you frequent updates throughout the week.

sources.news_title: Isaias forecast: Where the storm could hit the US
sources.text:
A tropical disturbance in the Gulf of Mexico is expected to develop into Tropical Storm Isaias within the next couple of days as forecasters closely monitor its path toward the United States.
The system could bring flooding rain, storm surge, damaging winds and isolated tornadoes to portions of the Gulf Coast later this week.
Communities from eastern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle are being urged to follow forecasts as confidence increases that the storm will approach the northern Gulf Coast by Friday or Saturday.
The National Hurricane Center is monitoring Invest 92L in the Bay of Campeche and has assigned it a high probability of tropical development.
Hurricane Hunter aircraft are scheduled to investigate the disturbance as meteorologists work to determine how quickly it strengthens and where it ultimately comes ashore.
NOAA's current forecast track and model guidance indicate the northern Gulf Coast remains the area of greatest concern.
Tropical Storm Isaias Spaghetti Models Point Toward Gulf Coast Landfall
Recent spaghetti model guidance shows a notable clustering of tracks across the northern Gulf Coast, with many solutions bringing Isaias ashore somewhere between eastern Louisiana and the Florida Panhandle. While individual models vary on the exact landfall point, forecasters say the consensus has become increasingly focused on that stretch of coastline.
Meteorologist Matt Devitt said Tuesday that the greatest potential for landfall currently appears to be from eastern Louisiana eastward to the Florida Panhandle.
Confidence is growing that Isaias will move toward the northern Gulf Coast, according to AccuWeather Lead Hurricane Meteorologist Alex DaSilva.
"There is still a low chance that the storm could slow down and meander in the Bay of Campeche, but that chance is shrinking," DaSilva told Newsweek.
While forecast uncertainty remains, AccuWeather's latest projection places the highest risk along portions of Mississippi and Alabama's coastline.
"The areas most at risk for landfall would be coastal Mississippi and coastal Alabama. We currently have landfall Saturday morning just east of Biloxi, MS," DaSilva said.
He added that forecasters should gain greater confidence in the storm's timing and exact landfall location once a defined circulation develops.
"Once a more well-established center of circulation forms during the next 24 hours, we should have more confidence on landfall timing and location."
The spread among models reflects lingering uncertainty about where the storm's center will form and how quickly it organizes, but several forecast tracks have shifted away from Mexico and toward the U.S. Gulf Coast over the past 24 hours.
Spaghetti models should not be interpreted as a prediction of impacts at a single point. Rather, they illustrate the range of possible paths a storm could take. Areas well east or west of the eventual center can still experience hazardous weather, particularly if the system develops an asymmetric structure.
Where Tropical Storm Isaias Could Make Landfall
Forecast steering currents are expected to pull the disturbance generally north-northeastward across the Gulf later this week. According to DaSilva, prevailing atmospheric winds favor a track toward the central Gulf Coast rather than a westward movement into Mexico.
Current projections suggest the highest probability of landfall lies near southeastern Louisiana, coastal Mississippi, Alabama's shoreline or the Florida Panhandle. Forecasters caution that even small track adjustments could substantially shift the zone of greatest impacts.
The storm's future path depends on several variables, including the exact location of its circulation center, surrounding atmospheric conditions and how rapidly it strengthens over open water. Systems that intensify more quickly often respond differently to steering patterns than weaker, less organized disturbances.
Residents across the northern Gulf Coast are being advised not to focus solely on the forecast center line. Tropical hazards frequently extend far from the point of landfall, particularly on the eastern side of a developing storm.
Could Tropical Storm Isaias Become a Hurricane?
Forecasters broadly agree that tropical development is likely, but questions remain about how strong Isaias may become before reaching the coast. Gulf water temperatures are sufficiently warm to support intensification, with sea-surface temperatures well above the threshold typically associated with tropical cyclone development.
Gulf water temperatures remain favorable for strengthening, but wind shear could ultimately determine how intense the storm becomes.
"Sea-surface temperatures in the Gulf are very conducive for intensification, however wind shear is likely to prevent significant intensification," DaSilva said.
He cautioned that the forecast could still change if environmental conditions become more favorable.
"This will need to be watched closely however as if the wind shear backs off or the storm moves more eastward, that can allow the storm to be in a more favorable environment for intensification."
AccuWeather expects Isaias to strengthen significantly while moving across the Gulf.
"We do expect that this storm will reach hurricane strength on Friday," DaSilva said.
However, he said increasing wind shear near the northern Gulf Coast could weaken the system before it reaches land.
"While we currently do not expect the storm to landfall as a hurricane, it cannot be ruled out if the interaction between the storm and wind shear is less than currently expected."
Hurricane Hunter aircraft are scheduled to investigate the disturbance Tuesday.
"The Hurricane Hunters will be flying into the storm later today. This should give us a better idea on the environment around the storm," DaSilva said.
A small number of scenarios still show the possibility of a stronger cyclone. Meteorologists stress that intensity forecasts remain more uncertain than track forecasts at this stage, making continued monitoring critical through midweek.
Flooding, Rain, Storm Surge and Tornado Threats Explained
Even if Isaias reaches hurricane strength, forecasters warn that water hazards may pose the greatest threat. The storm's expected structure could concentrate the heaviest rainfall east of the center, exposing parts of the Gulf Coast to flash flooding and rising rivers.
AccuWeather estimates that widespread rainfall totals could range from 1 to 4 inches, with localized amounts significantly higher in persistent rain bands. Some communities have already experienced repeated rounds of rainfall in recent days, increasing the risk of runoff problems and renewed flooding.
Storm surge is also a concern along vulnerable coastal areas. Persistent onshore winds can push water inland, causing inundation in low-lying areas even if the storm is not particularly intense. Coastal flooding may occur well before the center reaches land.
Forecasters say flooding rainfall remains the primary threat regardless of the storm's final intensity.
"The rainstorm is expected to bring a wide swath of 1-2 inches of rain, starting from the southern Gulf coast and the Bay of Campeche, northward into far eastern Louisiana and the Florida Panhandle," DaSilva said.
As the storm moves inland, impacts could extend well beyond the Gulf Coast.
"Heavy rain can spread into the Ohio Valley as far north as Kentucky and West Virginia, before moving eastward into the Carolinas and Virginia," he said.
The heaviest rainfall is forecast near and east of the expected landfall zone.
"A heavier swath of 4-8 inches is expected near where the storm makes landfall in southern and central Alabama and the Florida Panhandle, and also in southwestern North Carolina," DaSilva said.
Some areas could see much higher totals.
"The heaviest rain of 8-12 inches is expected to be across southern Alabama and southern Mississippi where the storm makes landfall, with an AccuWeather Local StormMax of 25 inches."
According to DaSilva, those amounts could trigger widespread flooding and other hazards.
"This rain can lead to widespread flooding and mudslides in any higher elevations of the Appalachians."
Strong winds are also expected close to where the center comes ashore.
"The storm will bring wind gusts of 40-60 mph close to where it makes landfall, including southwestern Alabama and the far western Florida Panhandle," DaSilva said.
Coastal communities could experience even stronger wind gusts.
"Along the coast close to landfall, wind gusts of 60-80 mph will also occur with an AccuWeather Local StormMax of 100 mph."
He warned those winds may be sufficient to down trees and power lines.
"These winds can cause power outages and some property damage, especially to areas close to the coast."
Tornadoes and storm surge are also concerns.
"We are also concerned about tropical tornadoes. Tornadoes will be possible this weekend," DaSilva said. "The most likely area to see tornadoes will be to the east of the center of circulation."
He added: "We also expect storm surge to occur near where the storm makes landfall."
What the National Hurricane Center Says Is Next
The National Hurricane Center continues to classify the system as Invest 92L while monitoring its organization in the southwestern Gulf. Development chances have increased as thunderstorm activity becomes more concentrated around the disturbance.
Hurricane Hunter aircraft reconnaissance is expected to provide a clearer picture of the storm's structure, strength and location. That information will feed directly into forecast models used by the NHC and other meteorological agencies.
If the disturbance acquires a well-defined circulation and sustained winds meet tropical-storm criteria, it would receive the name Isaias, becoming the ninth named storm of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season.
While the National Hurricane Center continues monitoring Invest 92L, DaSilva noted that key details about the storm's future track and impacts remain dependent on how quickly it organizes.
"Currently the NHC doesn't have a track or any impact polygons for this storm," he said.
Gulf Coast residents are being urged to review hurricane preparations before watches or warnings are issued.
"Gulf Coast residents should be checking their hurricane plans and making sure they have supplies ready to go," DaSilva said.
He also encouraged residents in vulnerable coastal areas to familiarize themselves with local evacuation guidance.
"It's always good to be over prepared than underprepared," he said. "It's also a good idea for coastal residents to check their evacuation zones, just in case they are called to evacuate by local emergency managers."

sources.news_title: Gulf system likely becoming Isaias soon, Houston impacts will be minimal
sources.text:
A tropical system is getting better organized in the Gulf and let’s dive into the latest data and most importantly, explain what it could mean for Southeast Texas.
Right now, Invest 92L has a 90% chance of becoming a tropical storm in the next two days. If it does strengthen into a tropical storm, the next name on the list is Isaias (ees-ah-EE-ahs).
The hurricane hunters are flying into the storm Tuesday morning, which should give us much better analysis (do we have a closed low, new atmospheric conditions, etc.) But the early guidance is beginning to give us a pretty good idea of where this system is headed.
And the good news for Houston is this...
It is not our storm. This the European AI forecast showing the center of circulation between Louisiana and Florida.
The cold front is the key:
There is an old meteorological saying that once the first real cold front moves through Southeast Texas, hurricane season is essentially over for us.
Obviously, hurricane season doesn’t officially end until November 30. But there is some meteorological truth behind the saying.
Think of that front as a brick wall.
Once the front moves through, the winds associated with it can block tropical systems from moving north into Southeast Texas. Instead, storms get steered either toward the west or, more commonly this time of year, toward the east.
That’s exactly what we’re seeing with this system.
Where the rain goes:
The system is expected to spend quite a bit of time hanging around the Bay of Campeche before finally moving. And here’s something important: the center of the circulation isn’t necessarily where the biggest impacts will be. As the system eventually moves north and east, the heavier rain shifts toward Louisiana and Florida. Some of the latest guidance is showing 5 to 9.5 inches of rain from Louisiana into parts of Florida.
Houston? Not much.
I’m putting a 20% chance of rain into the forecast Friday through Sunday because a few rainbands could potentially reach Southeast Texas, especially if the system becomes larger and less organized. But overall, I expect the heaviest rain to stay well east of us.
Could it become a hurricane?
This is where things get interesting.
The Gulf is incredibly warm right now, with water temperatures running roughly 84° to 88°. Those are record-setting warm temperatures in the Gulf, and warm water is certainly fuel for a tropical system.
Right now, temperatures and wind shear are both favorable for development.
Some of the guidance even shows a 30% to 40% probability of hurricane-force winds in the Bay of Campeche by Friday morning.
But that doesn’t mean we should expect a hurricane near Houston.
As the system moves north and east, it is going to run into increasing wind shear.
Wind shear is essentially a difference in wind speed and/or direction with height. Too much shear can tilt and disrupt a tropical cyclone, essentially ripping it apart.
In some circumstances, shear can actually help ventilate a storm and maintain its strength. But in this case, the increasing shear looks like another factor that will work against the system as it moves northeast.
So even if this system briefly becomes a hurricane over the Gulf, I expect it to weaken as it moves into stronger winds aloft.
And that brings us back to our cold front. The front and the changing wind pattern are helping steer this system away from Southeast Texas.
October tells us a lot:
I thought this statistic was fascinating. If you look at Texas hurricane landfalls from 1851 through 2025, Texas has had only three hurricane hits in the month of October.
One of them was Hurricane Jerry on October 15, 1989. Jerry made landfall at Jamaica Beach as a Category 1 hurricane and holds the distinction of being the latest hurricane landfall on record for both Texas and Southeast Texas.
Why does that matter?
Because by mid-October, the weather pattern across Texas is changing.
Those cold fronts become more frequent, and they can act as a barrier that keeps tropical systems from moving into Texas.
Florida is a completely different story.
If you look at the same historical data, Florida’s hurricane activity really increases from September to October.
That’s an important reminder that hurricane season doesn’t end everywhere at the same time. The atmospheric steering patterns change dramatically as we move deeper into fall.
And we’re seeing that play out right now with this Gulf system.

Forecast Models Show Isaias Reaching Category 1 in Gulf
sources.text:
Hurricane specialists are cautioning that a developing storm in the Gulf could strengthen into a hurricane this week as it moves toward the densely populated U.S. coastline.
The National Hurricane Center (NHC) says Tropical Storm Isaias could form at any time, assigning the system a 90 percent probability of becoming a tropical cyclone within 48 hours.
The disturbance is currently positioned just south of Texas in the southwestern Gulf of America. Updated forecast models indicate that Isaias could reach the United States by Saturday, potentially affecting Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama and Florida.
A forecasting model developed with Google’s DeepMind artificial intelligence technology places the odds of Isaias becoming at least a Category 1 hurricane at 57 percent. That classification requires sustained winds of more than 75 mph.
Forecasters also see a small possibility that the system could intensify rapidly into a major hurricane, defined as a Category 3 storm or stronger, with winds reaching at least 111 mph.
AccuWeather says hurricane-force winds could reach the U.S. Gulf Coast over the weekend, while the storm’s effects may extend well beyond the immediate landfall zone.
The weather service is forecasting widespread heavy rain and flooding across the Gulf Coast and Southeast. Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, Tennessee, the Carolinas and Florida’s Panhandle face the greatest risk.
Downpours, destructive wind gusts and isolated tornadoes could also affect Kentucky, West Virginia, Virginia, Maryland, Delaware and southern Ohio during the weekend.
Forecasters say the developing tropical system, which is expected to be named Isaias, could bring serious flooding to multiple Gulf Coast states (File Image)
The storm system is expected to become a tropical storm and could reach Category 1 hurricane strength before the week ends
As of Tuesday, the Atlantic had not produced a hurricane this year. AccuWeather Lead Hurricane Meteorologist Alex DaSilva said the current conditions still make it unlikely that Isaias will develop into an exceptionally powerful storm.
Even so, the system is expected to be strong enough to withstand the wind shear that has disrupted the development of other tropical storms this summer.
DaSilva said in a statement: “We anticipate that this area of showers and thunderstorms will overcome the wind shear and develop into either a tropical depression or tropical storm.”
He added that prevailing steering winds would most likely carry the system north-northeast toward the United States later this week, with landfall expected along the central Gulf Coast over the weekend.
Although powerful winds are working against the storm’s development, forecasters still expect its core to track across Alabama and nearby Gulf Coast states. Wind gusts of 40 to 60 mph could continue through Sunday.

As moisture bands move inland, some areas along the Gulf Coast, along with isolated locations in Georgia and North Carolina, could receive as much as eight inches of rain between now and October 12.
A broader region stretching from New Orleans to the Mid-Atlantic states of Maryland and Delaware could see between one and four inches of rainfall this week.
In its most severe projection, AccuWeather warns that the potential tropical storm could deliver up to 25 inches of rain across the hardest-hit parts of the South.
Meteorologists are warning of widespread flooding and intense rainfall across the Southeast this weekend
Google’s AI forecasting models estimate a 57 percent chance that Isaias will strengthen into a hurricane (Source: James Pettus/X)
If Isaias were to beat the odds and grow into a hurricane, it would set a new record for the latest date the first hurricane of the year formed.
There have only been two years on record in which a hurricane failed to develop in the Atlantic, 1907 and 1914.
The historic downturn in hurricane activity in the Atlantic this year has been fueled by the impact of a ‘super El Niño’ on the other side of the US.
El Niño is the widely used name for a natural weather phenomenon where sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean become abnormally warm.
This flips weather patterns around the globe, causing the normally chaotic hurricane season along the US East Coast to fizzle before storms have a chance to grow.
AccuWeather noted that the Gulf of America is still extremely warm and capable of providing the fuel for a tropical storm or hurricane to develop – with water temperatures hovering around a scorching 86 degrees Fahrenheit currently.
However, the increasing wind shear throughout the region has knocked down every storm which has formed during hurricane season, which ends on November 30.
Still, climate experts have previously warned that fast-moving tropical cyclones can erupt and reach major hurricane status in less than a week.
Ken Graham, the director of NOAA’s National Weather Service, warned before the 2025 hurricane season: ‘Every Category 5 [hurricane] that has ever hit this country was a tropical storm or less three days prior.’

Tropical Storm Isaias likely to form in Southwest Gulf
TAMPA, Fla. - A tropical disturbance developing in the Southwest Gulf could rapidly strengthen before encountering severe wind shear near the Northern Gulf Coast.
Gulf tropical system development
What we know:
A tropical disturbance known as Invest 92L is rapidly organizing in the Southwest Gulf.
Computer models indicate the system has a high probability of developing into Tropical Storm Isaias in the short term due to warm ocean temperatures.
However, strong wind shear across the northern Gulf is expected to tear the storm apart as it approaches the coastline.
Invest 92L tracker: Spaghetti models
What we don't know:
Forecasters cannot pinpoint the exact peak strength of the system before it reaches land.
While some computer models bring the disturbance to hurricane status during its brief window in warm waters, it remains uncertain how quickly wind shear will weaken the storm prior to landfall.
Storm track forecast path
Local perspective:
Current forecast models show no signs of an easterly turn toward the west coast of Florida.
Meteorologists are continuing to monitor the northern trajectory as the system drifts east-northeastward before heading north toward the Gulf Coast.

Tropical disturbance threatens Gulf Coast with wet weekend
Published 4:30 pm Monday, October 5, 2026
|                            Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...                        | 
The National Hurricane Center is monitoring an area of disturbed weather near Bayou Campeche that has an 80 percent chance of tropical development over the next seven days.
“We are past the climatological peak of hurricane season, but still well within it, so there is a risk,” said Donald Jones, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service’s Lake Charles office.
The system is currently an unorganized cluster of clouds, showers and thunderstorms, but Jones expects it to develop between Wednesday and Thursday. It is projected to make landfall along the northern Gulf Coast on Friday or over the weekend, setting up a wet few days for most of the Gulf Coast.
While southern Gulf water temperatures in the upper 80s are highly supportive of tropical activity, a cold front that moved through on Sunday has left strong upper-level wind shear sitting just offshore, Jones said. These strong west-to-east winds could tear the system apart as it moves north.
Jones said this shear may be the eliminating factor that keeps the storm from getting organized, leaving heavy rainfall as the primary threat.
Ahead of the system, local residents can expect dry conditions with temperatures climbing back to near 90 degrees by Wednesday.

Potential Tropical Threat Tracked In Gulf: What This Means For FL
Forecasters are keeping an eye on the Gulf, where Invest 92-L, which could strengthen into a tropical depression or storm, has popped up.
A potential tropical threat that popped up in the southwest Gulf over the weekend is being carefully watched by forecasters.
Invest 92-L, a trough of low pressure producing disorganized showers and thunderstorms on Monday afternoon, has a 60 percent chance of strengthening into a tropical depression or storm over the next two days and an 80 percent chance of strengthening within the week, the National Hurricane Center said.
“Although environmental conditions appear to be marginally conducive, gradual development is becoming more likely, and a tropical depression is expected to form during the middle portion of the week,” the NHC said. “This system is expected to drift eastward over the next couple of days, before it turns northward.”

If the system does develop, it could become Isaias, the ninth named storm of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season. It’s been an unusually quiet season, largely thanks to a strong El Niño climate pattern, which typically increases vertical wind shear, making it more difficult for tropical systems to organize and strengthen.
Though it’s too early to tell where the Invest 92-L might land, NHC forecasters said areas in the northern Gulf Coast should keep an eye on the system.
Find out what's happening in Tampafor free with the latest updates from Patch.
Denis Phillips, chief meteorologist for Tampa Bay 28, said in a social media post that there’s a “solid chance” that a tropical depression or Isaias forms by the weekend.
“Most models keep a weak, ragged rainmaker impacting the Northern Gulf Coast early next week. (Rain with a name),” Phillips wrote in the post. “A few, including the Google Deep Earth, make it stronger in the latest runs. Until we actually have a system to track, models will be all over the place.”
This system is the type forecasters expect to see at this time of year, Fox 13’s Paul Dellegatto wrote in a social media post. “Stalled frontal boundaries — like the one currently draped over the Gulf — frequently serve as a focal point for tropical development. Sea surface temperatures are more than warm enough and upper-level conditions favor thunderstorms, though increasing wind shear along the northern Gulf will be a limiting factor.”
Dellegatto continued, “If a system manages to get going, steering currents would favor a generally northward track. Regardless of whether a named storm forms, one thing is certain: elevated rain chances and above-normal rainfall will persist through mid-October.”

This potential storm comes with only two months left in the season, which ends at the end of November.
However, we are closely watching to see if we pass October 8, which would break a record for the latest first hurricane on record in a season.
Right now, there is a cluster of thunderstorms in the southwestern corner of the Gulf, off the coast of Mexico.
If the system does organize into a storm, Action News meteorologists say it has plenty of warm water to work with, as temperatures in the region are in the low to mid-80s.
Regardless of the outcome, the area is forecast to - at the very least - get some heavy rain along the Gulf Coast of Florida.

If that name sounds familiar, you might remember Tropical Storm Isaias in 2020, which caused major flooding in the Philadelphia area.

This system comes amid a particularly quiet Atlantic hurricane season. Typically, this far in hurricane season, we would expect to have an average of 14 named storms, seven hurricanes, with at least three being major hurricanes.
However, so far this year, there have only been eight named storms and zero hurricanes.
One came close but didn't quite reach the 74 mph status needed to be considered a hurricane.
Action News Meteorologist Karen Rogers says El Niño is why it has been so abnormally quiet.
With El Niño, in the Atlantic Basin, there is increased vertical wind shear, where the tops of the storms are "blown off," preventing storms from forming, Rogers explains.
If the season ends with zero hurricanes, it would match records that were set over 100 years ago. There have only been two seasons where there have been no hurricanes and those were in 1907 and 1914.

Flood-weary communities across the Southeast could face another soaking this weekend as a disturbance in the Gulf threatens to develop into Tropical Storm Isaias.

The threat comes as an earlier round of downpours leaves parts of the region vulnerable to renewed flooding.
National Weather Service flood watches covered portions of Florida, southern Alabama and Georgia on Monday, with several remaining in effect through the evening. Forecasters in Tallahassee called for another 2 to 4 inches of rain across much of their forecast area, with localized amounts reaching 6 inches.
For some communities, the next storm could arrive before the ground has a chance to dry out.
AccuWeather warned that parts of the Southeast could receive as much as 14 inches of rain this weekend. Flooding could develop even if the Gulf disturbance fails to become a named storm.

sources.news_title: Tropical depression forms in the Gulf, forecast to strengthen into first hurricane of Atlantic season
sources.text:
Tropical Depression Nine has formed in the southwestern Gulf and is forecast to become a hurricane, potentially bringing significant flooding rain and strong winds to parts of the northern Gulf Coast and South late this week.
The system is expected to become Tropical Storm Isaias (ees-ah-EE-ahs) soon and strengthen into a hurricane on Thursday. That will make Isaias the first hurricane of an Atlantic season squashed by El Niño.
Get live updates and alerts. Download the CNN Weather app.
Depression Nine has winds of 35 mph and is located about 630 miles southwest of the Louisiana coast.
The system will quickly track north, bringing with it flooding rain, powerful winds and storm surge, likely impacting areas from southern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle. It’s expected to reach Category 2 strength as it heads toward the coast.
Exactly where the storm could track or how strong it will be when it approaches land are still not set in stone, but anyone along the Gulf Coast from Louisiana to Florida’s Big Bend needs to monitor the forecast closely.
Forecast uncertainty
Gulf water is record warm for this time of year, primed to help fuel any system, but atmospheric conditions may limit the storm’s strength before moving ashore.
The current forecast shows the tropical depression strengthening into a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 100 mph.
Wind shear — changes in wind speed or direction at different levels of the atmosphere — is low in the southern Gulf, which will allow the system to thrive and reach this strength. Higher, storm-killing wind shear is in place closer to the Gulf Coast, which will weaken the system as it makes its approach.
But the system is also forecast to move quickly, so its exposure to the higher wind shear may be limited. If the storm were to move slower, it could weaken quickly as it meanders in hostile conditions.
No matter its final fate, heavy rain is a concern on the Gulf Coast and in other parts of the South by late this week.
As this year has already shown, it doesn’t take a hurricane-strength system to cause significant impacts, particularly in a warming world that’s making tropical systems wetter.
Tropical storms Arthur and Edouard didn’t last long, but their heavy rain resulted in significant flash flooding and water rescues. Parts of Louisiana and Mississippi took the brunt of Arthur’s flooding while Edouard dropped over 20 inches of rain in eastern Texas.
Parts of Alabama, Georgia, the Florida Panhandle, southeast Louisiana and Mississippi are most at risk of heavy rain from this system. The downpours could start to ramp up along the coast as soon as Friday and then continue to soak the region while creeping farther inland through the weekend.
Several inches of rain could fall, but it’s too soon to pinpoint which locations might see the most and could experience flash flooding.
Pinning down the location and severity of any storm surge flooding, strong winds and tornadoes along the northern Gulf Coast is even more difficult this far out in time because we need to know how strong the storm will be and exactly where it will track. The earliest those impacts could arrive is late Friday or Saturday.
What’s typical in October and November
Four named storms — that’s tropical storm strength or greater — typically form in October and November, but some hurricane seasons can have a stronger finish while others quiet down.
The last few years illustrate this year-to-year ebb and flow. Seven storms formed during October and November in 2024, but just two formed during the same time in 2023.
Late-season storms tend to form closer to the United States, including in the Gulf, Caribbean and off the Southeast coast, which makes them more likely to impact land.
While there are usually fewer storms, they can still be destructive.
Last year, Category 5 Hurricane Melissa devastated Jamaica in October’s final week.
Hurricane Michael roared into the Florida Panhandle on October 10, 2018, becoming the latest landfalling Category 5 on record in the US. And Hurricane Sandy may be the most notorious of all: It morphed into a hybrid superstorm in late-October 2012 and walloped the East Coast.
Super El Niño’s grip on the Atlantic basin means a repeat of notorious late-season hurricanes is less likely this year. Its storm-killing wind is the main reason this season could go hurricane-free for the first time in reliable records.
